paragraphs: Soon after getting his four-year-old Mitya off his hands, Fyodor Pavlovitch married again. The marriage lasted eight years. His second wife, Sofya Ivanovna, was also a very young girl. He found her in another province, where he had gone on some small piece of business with a Jew. Fyodor Pavlovitch was a drunkard and a vicious debauchee, but he never failed to invest his capital, and he ran his business affairs very successfully, though, no doubt, without too many scruples. Sofya Ivanovna was the daughter of an obscure deacon. She had been an orphan with no relations since early childhood. She grew up in the house of a general’s widow, a wealthy old lady of good standing, who was at once her benefactress and her tormentor. I do not know the details. I have only heard that the orphan girl, a meek and gentle creature, was once cut down from a noose that she had tied to a nail in the loft. That was how badly she suffered from the whims and endless nagging of this old woman, who was apparently not bad-hearted, but had turned into an unbearable tyrant out of sheer idleness.

Fyodor Pavlovitch proposed to her. People asked about him, and he was turned down. But, just as with his first wife, he then suggested to the orphan girl that they elope. There is little doubt that she would never have married him if she had learned a little more about him in time. But she lived in another province, and besides, what could a girl of sixteen know, except that she would rather be at the bottom of the river than stay with her benefactress? So the poor child swapped a benefactress for a benefactor. Fyodor Pavlovitch got not a penny this time, because the general’s widow was furious. She gave them nothing and cursed them both. But he had never counted on a dowry. What had tempted him was the girl’s remarkable beauty, and above all her look of innocence. That look had a peculiar pull on a vicious profligate who, until then, had only admired the coarser kinds of feminine beauty.

“Those innocent eyes slit my soul up like a razor,” he used to say later, with his loathsome snigger. In so depraved a man, of course, that might mean no more than lust. Since he had got no dowry with his wife, and had, so to speak, taken her “from the noose,” he did not bother to be polite to her. He made her feel she had “wronged” him. Her extraordinary meekness and submissiveness gave him the chance to trample on the most basic decencies of married life. He brought loose women into his house and held drunken orgies in front of his wife. To show how far things went, I should mention that Grigory sided with the new mistress. He was a gloomy, stupid, stubborn, argumentative servant who had always hated his first mistress, Adelaïda Ivanovna. Now he took up the new wife’s cause. He abused Fyodor Pavlovitch in a way that hardly became a servant, and once he broke up the revels and chased all the disorderly women out of the house. In the end this unhappy young woman, who had lived in terror since childhood, fell ill with the kind of nervous disease found most often in peasant women, who are said to be “possessed by devils.” After terrible fits of hysterics she sometimes even lost her reason. Yet she bore Fyodor Pavlovitch two sons, Ivan and Alexey, the first in the first year of the marriage and the second three years later. When she died, little Alexey was in his fourth year. Strange as it sounds, I know he remembered his mother for the rest of his life, like a dream, of course. At her death, almost exactly the same thing happened to the two little boys as to their elder brother Mitya. Their father forgot them completely and abandoned them. The same Grigory looked after them, and they lived in his cottage. That is where the tyrannical old lady who had raised their mother found them. She was still alive, and in all those eight years she had never forgotten the insult done to her. All that time she had been getting exact reports on how her Sofya lived. When she heard of the girl’s illness and her hideous surroundings, she announced to her servants, two or three times, out loud:
“It serves her right. God has punished her for her ingratitude.”

Exactly three months after Sofya Ivanovna’s death, the general’s widow suddenly turned up in our town and drove straight to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house. She spent only half an hour in the town, but she got a great deal done. It was evening. Fyodor Pavlovitch, who hadn’t seen her in those eight years, came in to meet her drunk. The story goes that the moment she saw him, without a word of explanation, she gave him two good, resounding slaps across the face, grabbed him by a tuft of hair, and shook him up and down three times. Then, without a word, she went straight to the cottage where the two boys were. At the first glance she saw that they were unwashed and in dirty linen, and at once she boxed Grigory’s ears as well. She announced that she was taking both children away, wrapped them up just as they were in a rug, put them in her carriage, and drove off to her own town. Grigory took the blow like a devoted slave, without a word. As he showed the old lady out to her carriage, he gave her a low bow and said solemnly that “God would repay her for the orphans.” “You are a blockhead all the same,” the old lady shouted at him as she drove away.

Fyodor Pavlovitch thought it over and decided this was all for the best. He gave the general’s widow his formal consent to whatever she proposed for his children’s education. As for the slaps she had given him, he drove all over town telling the story.

As it turned out, the old lady died soon afterward, but in her will she left the boys a thousand roubles each “for their instruction, and so that all be spent on them exclusively, with the condition that it be so portioned out as to last till they are twenty-one, for it is more than adequate provision for such children. If other people think fit to throw away their money, let them.” I have not read the will myself, but I heard that there was something odd of the kind in it, very whimsically worded. The main heir was Yefim Petrovitch Polenov, the Marshal of Nobility of the province, and he proved to be an honest man. He wrote to Fyodor Pavlovitch and saw right away that there was nothing to be got out of him for the children’s education. (Fyodor Pavlovitch never actually said no, but only stalled, as he always did in such cases, and was even, at times, gushingly sentimental.) So Yefim Petrovitch took an interest in the orphans himself. He grew especially fond of the younger one, Alexey, who lived for a long time as a member of his family. I ask the reader to note this from the start. The young people owed their schooling and upbringing to Yefim Petrovitch more than to anyone else. He was a man of a generosity and humanity one rarely meets. He left the two thousand roubles that the general’s widow had left them untouched, so that by the time they came of age, the interest had doubled their shares. He paid for both their educations out of his own pocket, and he certainly spent far more than a thousand roubles on each. I will not give a detailed account of their boyhood and youth, only a few of the most important events. About the elder, Ivan, I will say only that he grew into a rather sullen, reserved boy, though far from timid. At ten he had understood that they lived not in their own home but on other people’s charity, and that their father was a man it was shameful to speak of. From very early on, almost from infancy (so they say, at least), the boy showed a brilliant and unusual talent for learning. I don’t know exactly why, but he left Yefim Petrovitch’s family when he was barely thirteen, and went to a Moscow gymnasium, where he boarded with an experienced and famous teacher who was an old friend of Yefim Petrovitch. Ivan used to say later that it was all because of Yefim Petrovitch’s “ardor for good works.” Yefim Petrovitch was carried away by the idea that a boy of genius ought to be trained by a teacher of genius. But by the time the young man finished at the gymnasium and entered the university, neither Yefim Petrovitch nor this teacher was alive. Yefim Petrovitch had made no arrangement for paying out the tyrannical old lady’s legacy, which had grown from one thousand to two. The money was held up by the red tape that is unavoidable in Russia, and for his first two years at the university the young man was hard pressed, because he had to keep himself the whole time he was studying. It should be noted that he did not even try to contact his father. Perhaps this was pride, or contempt. Perhaps it was cool common sense, which told him he would get no real help from such a father. Whatever the reason, the young man was not at all downhearted, and he found work. At first he gave lessons at sixpence an hour, and later he placed short items about street incidents in the newspapers, signed “Eye-Witness.” These items, it was said, were so lively and spicy that the papers soon took them. This alone showed the young man’s practical and intellectual superiority over the crowds of needy, unlucky students of both sexes who haunt the offices of newspapers and journals, unable to think of anything better than endless begging for copying work and translations from the French. Once Ivan Fyodorovitch had made contact with the editors, he always kept it up. In his later years at the university he published brilliant reviews of books on various specialized subjects, and became well known in literary circles. But only in his last year did he suddenly catch the attention of a much wider readership, so that a great many people noticed him and remembered him. It was a rather curious episode. He had just left the university and was getting ready to go abroad on his two thousand roubles, when Ivan Fyodorovitch published a strange article in one of the major journals. It attracted general notice. The subject was one he could have been supposed to know nothing about, since he was a student of natural science. It dealt with a question being debated everywhere at the time: the status of the ecclesiastical courts. After going through several opinions on the matter, he went on to give his own view. What struck people most about the article was its tone and its unexpected conclusion. Many in the Church party took him without question as one of their own. Yet the secularists, and even atheists, joined them in applauding him. In the end, some shrewd people suggested that the article was nothing but an impudent satirical burlesque. I mention this episode in particular because the article made its way into the famous monastery in our neighborhood. The monks there took a special interest in the question of the ecclesiastical courts, and the article left them completely bewildered. When they learned the author’s name, they were interested to find that he was a native of our town and the son of “that Fyodor Pavlovitch.” And just then the author himself showed up among us.

Why Ivan Fyodorovitch had come to us, I remember asking myself at the time with some uneasiness. That fateful visit was the first step toward so many consequences, and I have never fully explained it to myself. It seemed strange on the face of it. Here was a young man so learned, so proud, and apparently so careful, suddenly visiting an infamous house and a father who had ignored him all his life. The father hardly knew him, never gave him a thought, and would not have given him money under any circumstances, though he was always afraid that his sons Ivan and Alexey would turn up asking for it. And now the young man was staying in the house of such a father. He had been living there for two months, and the two got on perfectly. Many others besides me were astonished by this last fact. Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, who has been mentioned already, the cousin of Fyodor Pavlovitch’s first wife, happened to be in the neighborhood again, visiting his estate. He had come from Paris, where he lived permanently. I remember that he was more surprised than anyone when he met the young man. Ivan interested him greatly. Sometimes he argued with him, and not without an inner pang he measured his own learning against Ivan’s.

“He is proud,” he used to say. “He will never be short of pennies. He has money enough to go abroad right now. What does he want here? Anyone can see he hasn’t come for money, because his father would never give him any. He has no taste for drink and dissipation, and still his father can’t do without him. They get on so well together!”

That was the truth. The young man had a clear hold over his father, who really did seem to be behaving more decently, and at times even seemed ready to do as his son said, though he was often extremely, even spitefully, contrary.

We learned only later that Ivan had come partly at the request, and in the interest, of his elder brother Dmitri. He met Dmitri for the first time on this visit, though before leaving Moscow he had corresponded with him about an important matter that mattered more to Dmitri than to himself. The reader will learn in due time exactly what that business was. Even after I knew about this particular circumstance, though, Ivan Fyodorovitch still struck me as an enigmatic figure, and his visit still seemed rather mysterious to me.
I may add that Ivan then looked like a go-between for his father and his elder brother Dmitri. Dmitri was in open quarrel with their father and was even planning to sue him.

The family, I repeat, was now together for the first time, and some of its members were meeting for the first time in their lives. The younger brother, Alexey, had already been among us a year, having been the first of the three to arrive. It is about this brother Alexey that I find it hardest to speak in this introduction. Still, I must give some preliminary account of him, if only to explain one queer fact: I have to present my hero to the reader in the cassock of a novice. Yes, he had spent the past year in our monastery, and seemed willing to be shut up there for the rest of his life.
